summary:
I migrated BudgetTracker's database off MSSQL and onto Postgres — a full Drizzle ORM rewrite rather than a compatibility shim, since the app was still single-user and this was the window to make breaking changes cleanly. The production data (8,239 transactions, 773 merchants) moved in one cut. While I was in there I also shipped the app as an installable PWA with an offline read-cache, which took some care with the service worker: the AI assistant streams over server-sent events, so the SW had to exclude `/api` paths while still precaching the app shell.

The AI Insights chat used to be a single completion over a pre-baked context block, which meant it declined anything requiring a real lookup ("how much on vaping in May"). Now it runs an agent loop with a list_transactions tool that accepts arrays of search terms — one call per concept query rather than one per synonym. While working on that I also built income pattern detection: the system scans historical deposits, clusters them by merchant and interval, and proposes confirmed paycheck schedules for the cash flow projection. The live test found my employer's biweekly deposit with 100% confidence across 98 transactions; it also surfaced the same employer under an older merchant name from a few years back, which I dismissed.

A security audit in early June caught a path traversal in the receipt upload endpoint — `..%2F`-encoded sequences could escape the upload directory, meaning any authenticated user could read arbitrary server files. I also separated JWT access and refresh token types (a refresh token was technically usable as a Bearer access token), added an SSRF guard on user-supplied LLM base URLs enforcing a public-HTTPS-only boundary while keeping the server's own local model exempt, and wired magic-byte content verification on uploads so the declared MIME type can't be spoofed. All four phases shipped to production without a schema migration.

I built a read-only MCP tool surface on top of BudgetTracker — 13 tools covering upcoming obligations, burn rate, cash flow projection, spending anomalies, subscriptions, and more. The constraint I wanted to hold throughout was that the LLM reasons over pre-computed SQL results and never does the arithmetic itself. Those tools are registered in my home assistant and now feed the morning briefing: each morning a database call returns yesterday's spend, today's per-account totals, and a 14-day run-rate forecast, phrased by a local model so the financial figures never leave the LAN.

highlights.oneLiner: Migrated DB to Postgres/Drizzle, added income pattern detection, MCP tool surface, and security fixes
Swapped brain to Qwen3.6-35B, trimmed toolset 32K→20K tokens, added spending section to morning brief
Morning briefing gains a Spending section sourced from BudgetTracker MCP, phrased by local model
